docs.title: NIH SBIR Proposal Guide for Health Companies
docs.text:
A health company with strong preliminary data can still leave an NIH review round without a score if reviewers can't follow how its aims lead to a product. Only about half the applications in each SBIR round are discussed and scored. Since 2026, each attempt also counts against an HHS limit of nine applications per company a year, and NIH no longer accepts a late submission. An unscored application now costs a slot as well as a cycle. Decide which projects deserve those slots before drafting begins, then build each application around the criteria reviewers score.

docs.title: Application Planner
docs.text:
HHS accepts nine SBIR and STTR applications per company in each fiscal year, and the count covers new and resubmitted Phase I, Fast-Track and Direct to Phase II applications as well as contract proposals (NOT-OD-26-090). Enter every application your company plans for fiscal 2027 to see how many slots remain and the earliest month each award could start.

ProjectTypeReceipt dateEarliest startCounts No applications added yet.

Fiscal 2027 runs from October 1, 2026 to September 30, 2027. Earliest start dates come from the review cycles in PA-27-100, which expires on April 6, 2027. A standard Phase II after an awarded Phase I is not among the application types NOT-OD-26-090 lists, so the planner leaves it out of the count. Your entries stay in this browser and are never sent anywhere.

docs.title: Before You Write
docs.text: A company can win on merit and still lose the award if its ownership or headcount has shifted by the award date. NIH tests eligibility at the time of award for both Phase I and Phase II, and the principal investigator's employment must hold through the whole project (PA-27-100). Settle ownership questions with counsel before the first draft.

docs.title: Eligibility
docs.text: NIH funds only US for-profit small business concerns that employ no more than 500 people, counting every affiliate, and that operate primarily within the United States. Ownership must be more than 50% held by US citizens or permanent residents, by other qualifying small businesses, or by an Indian tribe, ANC or NHO. Venture-backed companies qualify when several investment firms together hold the majority and no single firm holds more than half. A company in that position must attach a signed certification saved under the exact file name "SBIR Application VCOC Certification.pdf", since a renamed file can delay processing.

docs.title: SBIR or STTR
docs.text: The route depends on who does the work. Under SBIR, your company normally carries out at least two thirds of Phase I research and half of Phase II, with partners and consultants taking the rest. STTR is built for projects that depend on a formal collaboration with a university or other nonprofit research institution. The partner must perform at least 30% of the work and your company at least 40%, and the principal investigator can be employed by either side (NIH SEED). The award goes to your company under both programs. SBIR carries a far larger share of NIH money, with 3.2% of the extramural research budget against 0.45% for STTR, so choose STTR only when the partnership is real.

docs.title: Choosing a Phase
docs.text:
Reviewers judge a Phase I application on whether its strategy will establish feasibility, manage the riskiest steps and set measurable milestones to reach before Phase II. Phase I normally lasts six months. Fast-Track combines both phases in one application, which suits a team that can already write a full Phase II plan and wants to close the funding gap between awards. If feasibility is already proven with other funding, Direct to Phase II skips the first phase altogether. After a Phase I award, keep Phase II eligibility by applying within the first six due dates after the Phase I budget period ends.

1Does the project depend on a formal collaboration with a university or other nonprofit research institution? YesSTTRYour company does at least 40% of the work and the partner at least 30%. NoSBIRYour company does at least two thirds of Phase I work and half of Phase II. 2Has feasibility already been shown with other funding? YesDirect to Phase IISkip Phase I and apply for up to two years of development. NoGo to question 3 3Can your team write a full Phase II plan today? YesFast-TrackBoth phases in one application, with no funding gap between them. NoPhase ISix months of feasibility work, ending in the milestones Phase II needs.

docs.title: Choosing an Institute
docs.text: NIH's Center for Scientific Review assigns every application to an institute, and you can request one on the PHS Assignment Request Form. Each institute publishes its own research priorities, budget waiver topics and contacts on NIH's Small Business Funding Considerations page. Call the program officer before writing. The program officer can confirm fit, point you to a better institute and tell you whether your study counts as a clinical trial under NIH's definition (sbir.org).

docs.title: Registrations
docs.text:
Four accounts must be active before submission, and failing to finish them in time is not accepted as a reason for lateness.

  • SAM.gov - issues your Unique Entity Identifier, and the registration has to be renewed every year.
  • SBA Company Registry - issues the SBC Control ID you enter on the SBIR/STTR Information form.
  • eRA Commons - needs at least one Signing Official and one principal investigator account. A PI who also signs for the company needs two separate accounts, and every PI profile must link to an ORCID ID.
  • Grants.gov - opens only once SAM.gov registration is active.

NIH estimates six weeks or more for the full set, including three weeks or more for a first SAM.gov registration and two weeks or more for eRA Commons.

docs.title: Compliance Matrix
docs.text:
An application with the strongest science in its review group can still be withdrawn from funding consideration over 10-point body text, a password-protected PDF or a line typed into the margin (NIH format rules). No reviewer is involved in any of it. NIH systems catch many of these faults at submission, and Center for Scientific Review staff screen every application for completeness and compliance before it reaches a study section (PA-27-100). Give the final check to someone who didn't write the science and will read each page the way an auditor would.

Download the one-page checklist (PDF)

docs.title: Formatting Rules for Every PDF
docs.text:
• Font size - 11 points or larger for body text. Text inside figures can run smaller as long as it stays legible at 100% zoom.
  • Type density - no more than 15 characters per linear inch and six lines per vertical inch.
  • Fonts - Arial, Georgia, Helvetica and Palatino Linotype all meet the standard, and any other font that passes the size and density rules is accepted.
  • Page and margins - letter-size pages with margins of at least half an inch on every side. Keep everything you supply out of the margins.
  • Headers and footers - leave both off your files, because NIH adds its own when it assembles the application.
  • Security - switch off every PDF security feature. NIH systems have to open each file, so passwords and encryption aren't allowed.
  • Flattening - flatten any PDF that has fillable fields, layers or inserted elements, since an unflattened file can trigger an eRA Commons error.
  • Signatures - an electronic signature can't stay live in an attachment. Sign the document, then flatten it.
  • Scans - create text documents in a word processor and convert them to PDF. Scan only signed pages, such as letters of support.
  • File names - keep each to 50 characters or fewer, unique within the application and free of ampersands.
  • Links - URLs are allowed only where the announcement or form instructions permit them, and the URL itself has to be the visible link text.

docs.title: Page Limits at a Glance
docs.text:
Section Phase I (R43) Phase II, Fast-Track, Direct to Phase II (R44) Project Summary/Abstract 30 lines 30 lines Project Narrative 3 sentences 3 sentences Specific Aims 1 page 1 page Research Strategy 6 pages 12 pages Commercialization Plan Not allowed 12 pages Introduction to a resubmission 1 page 1 page Regulatory Plan, clinical trials only 2 pages 2 pages

Limits are from NIH's Table of Page Limits, and the Regulatory Plan limit is from PA-27-100.

docs.title: Form Entries That Block Submission
docs.text:
Each principal investigator's eRA Commons ID goes in the Credential field of the Senior/Key Person Profile, and without a valid ID the application can't be submitted electronically. The Unique Entity Identifier on the application has to match the one held in SAM.gov and in your eRA Commons organization profile. If you answer "Yes" to human subjects on the R&R Other Project Information form, you'll need at least one study record or a Delayed Onset Study record.

Trial applications attach the Regulatory Plan as "RegulatoryPlan.pdf" under Other Attachments on that same form. Any company that already holds an SBIR Phase II award from a federal agency must add its Phase II commercialization history (NIH Form G.440). PA-27-100 drops the Data Management and Sharing Plan, though Resource Sharing Plans still follow the Application Guide.

docs.title: Overlap and Duplication Rules
docs.text:
NIH won't accept essentially identical applications filed at the same time under PA-27-100 and another HHS announcement, and the STTR parent counts as one of those. Resubmissions run on their own clock. An A1 can't go in until NIH has issued the summary statement for the A0, and a new application can't go in while an overlapping one is still waiting for its summary statement. NIH also refuses derivative applications that propose the same product with non-substantive changes for different uses.

Paying for work abroad has its own rule. Any subaward or subcontract to a foreign entity makes the application noncompliant. Unfunded foreign collaborators, foreign consultants and equipment bought from foreign vendors are still allowed.

NIH makes the applicant responsible for viewing the assembled application in eRA Commons before the due date. Set aside time on the last day for one full read of that version.

docs.title: Funded Abstract Teardown
docs.text: NINR tells first-time applicants to study sample SBIR and STTR applications (NINR), but few companies publish theirs. Funded abstracts fill part of that gap. The three awards below come from medical devices, diagnostics and digital health, and each was funded at a different stage, which changes what its abstract had to prove.

docs.title: Rivanna: Ultrasound Guidance for Pediatric Lumbar Puncture
docs.text:
NCI, R44CA302033, Direct to Phase II, $2.21 million, announced September 2025 (VABio)

Up to 38% of lumbar punctures are traumatic, with blood contaminating the spinal fluid, and the complication is linked to poorer outcomes. Rivanna applies that rate to children who can't avoid the procedure. Acute lymphoblastic leukemia makes up about a quarter of pediatric cancer cases, and a child in treatment may undergo up to 20 lumbar punctures over two years. A risk counted per procedure becomes a burden each patient carries again and again.

The product adds pediatric features to Rivanna's existing Accuro 3S ultrasound platform, using AI to find spinal anatomy and guide the needle. NIH had already funded the company's earlier work on bedside spinal navigation for lumbar puncture, and that record is what supports skipping Phase I. Its aims stay preclinical, testing usability, accuracy and how quickly clinicians learn the system.

docs.title: Leuko Labs: Needle-Free Neutropenia Monitoring
docs.text:
NCI, 2R44CA228920-04, Phase IIB, $1,702,979 in fiscal 2024 (NIH project record)

Scale comes first. About 850,000 US cancer patients receive chemotherapy each year, and neutropenia costs an estimated $6.4 billion annually. PointCheck images the capillaries under the fingernail to detect severe neutropenia without drawing blood, so patients can check at home between chemotherapy cycles.

Prior evidence is counted in patients, from a 44-patient proof-of-concept study to usability and feasibility studies with 154 and 193 subjects. The remaining aims run from pilot production of 20 units through a 210-patient pivotal study and a Class II De Novo submission to FDA, ending with a 50-patient outcomes study to support reimbursement. After each aim, a reviewer can see exactly where the device will stand with regulators and payers, in a project that began in July 2018.

docs.title: Nest Genomics: Hereditary Cancer Care Inside the Health Record
docs.text:
NHGRI, STTR, 1R42HG013908-01, $291,643 in fiscal 2024 (NIH project record)

The gap Nest Genomics targets opens after diagnosis. About 4% of the US population carries inherited cancer risk, and identifying those patients has improved, but long-term care lags behind. Uptake of recommended surveillance ranges from 52% to 85% depending on the test, and uptake of risk-reducing surgery ranges from 9% to 65%. Adherence falls over time, and it falls fastest among adolescents and young adults moving between schools, jobs and clinicians.

Hereditary cancer was a deliberate starting point. Testing for it is guideline-recommended and well covered by payers. The platform stores structured genetic results in the electronic medical record and gives clinicians decision support for guideline-based care plans. It also automates charting and adds a mobile tool for patients. The public record cuts off before the full list of aims.

Search NIH RePORTER by your target institute and activity code for recent awards in your product category, and note which numbers each abstract puts in its opening lines.

docs.title: How Reviewers Score
docs.text: A strong peer review score doesn't guarantee an award. Recommended applications go to a second review by the institute's national Advisory Council. NIH then weighs scientific merit against available funds, the project's fit with institute priorities and any security risk found through the HHS Due Diligence Program (PA-27-100). Of those factors, only merit can be shaped on the page, and reviewers build it from five separate scores and one overall impact score.

docs.title: Five Scored Criteria
docs.text:
Each criterion gets its own score, but NIH tells reviewers an application doesn't have to be strong in all five. It even notes that a project with little innovation may still be what a field needs to advance.

  • Significance - reviewers ask whether the product meets an important unmet need and how clinical practice will change if the aims succeed. Leuko Labs answers with 850,000 patients a year and $6.4 billion in costs before it describes the device.
  • Investigators - once a project nears market, the scientific résumé is no longer enough. For later-stage work, reviewers also ask whether the team has the expertise to commercialize the product.
  • Innovation - Phase II and Fast-Track reviewers ask for a credible plan to put a time barrier between the company and rivals building a similar solution. Intellectual property protection is part of that answer.
  • Approach - a Phase II application has to show progress against Phase I objectives, or their equivalent for a Direct to Phase II. Rivanna's request rests on NIH-funded navigation work completed before the award.
  • Environment - the business setting counts alongside the lab. A Phase I company is asked whether it has business expertise and resources, or has identified where it will find them.

docs.title: Commercialization Plan Questions
docs.text:
Reviewers of Phase II and Fast-Track applications weigh the Commercialization Plan in the overall impact score, though it gets no score of its own. Their first question is whether the company understands the barriers between its product and the market, such as regulatory approval, insurance reimbursement, competing products and customer preferences, and has a strategy for each. Leuko Labs builds two of those strategies into its aims, a De Novo submission to FDA and an outcomes study to support reimbursement. Nest Genomics avoided the reimbursement question by starting where payer coverage already exists.

Reviewers also look for post-SBIR milestones, a funding plan and any letters of interest or commitment that back it. Venture-backed companies should expect one more question. Where a project duplicates well-funded private development, reviewers ask why federal money is needed despite the private investment already behind it.

docs.title: After Review
docs.text: A Just-in-Time request asks for information before an award decision. NIH states that the request is neither a Notice of Award nor an indicator of possible funding. Hold back on new hires and spending until the Notice of Award arrives, because any costs incurred before then are at your own risk.

docs.title: Resubmission
docs.text: NIH allows one resubmission of any application, and it's the only point where you can answer reviewers on the record (NOT-OD-18-197). If the A1 fails, the project can come back as a new application. That new version may not mention earlier reviewers, respond to their critiques or show how the project has changed. Every argument you hold back from the A1 loses its context once the A1 is used.

docs.title: Reading the Summary Statement
docs.text:
The summary statement reaches eRA Commons after peer review, and the program official's name and contact details sit at the top. Call that person before you decide anything. NIH SEED suggests using the call to test whether the reviewers' comments are addressable, how you plan to answer them and how to fit the most important responses onto one page (NIH SEED).

Sort each criticism by the criterion it hits. Concerns about the Approach, such as a missing control, a thin alternative strategy or an unclear milestone, can usually be fixed with new data or a redesigned aim. Concerns about Significance or Innovation question whether the project deserves funding at all, and a one-page reply rarely changes that verdict.

docs.title: Revising or Starting Over
docs.text: An A1 has to go in within 37 months of the original application. If you choose a new application instead, NIH doesn't require the science to be substantially different. It has to be formatted as new, with no Introduction, no reference to earlier reviews and no marked changes. Revise when the critique centers on execution and you can answer it with evidence. Start over when reviewers doubted the problem or the product, because a new application reaches a panel that hasn't already formed a view.

docs.title: Writing the Introduction
docs.text:
The Introduction is a one-page attachment. NIH SEED recommends that it thank reviewers for their comments, answer each concern raised in the summary statement and summarize the substantial additions, deletions and changes to the application. Quote or paraphrase each criticism, then state what changed and where in the application a reviewer will find it. Reviewers judge the application as now presented, taking into account your responses and the changes made (PA-27-100).

Changes stay unmarked in the body of the application. For applications due from May 25, 2024, NIH has told applicants not to flag edits with markup such as bracketing, indenting or highlighting, and to outline changes only in the Introduction (NOT-OD-24-061). Before the program official call, draft the Introduction in outline form, one line per criticism, so the conversation centers on the responses that need the most space.

docs.text: All sources were last checked on November 10, 2026. NIH notices and announcements take precedence over any summary in the guide, so confirm a rule against the live notice before you rely on it.

docs.title: What Changed in 2026
docs.text: Any SBIR plan, template or checklist drafted before April 2026 rests on submission rules that NIH has since replaced. Program authority expired on October 1, 2025, and on November 17 NIH withdrew every open SBIR and STTR announcement with immediate effect (NOT-OD-26-006). Congress restored both programs through September 30, 2031 under a law signed on April 13, 2026 (S. 3971), and NIH reopened submissions on August 5 under two new parent announcements, PA-27-100 and PA-27-102. Several rules came back stricter than before.

docs.title: Nine Applications Across HHS
docs.text: A company that resubmits two applications and files Fast-Track for a third has used a third of its year before any new idea is written. HHS counts new and resubmitted Phase I, Fast-Track and Direct to Phase II applications against a single limit of nine per fiscal year, shared by NIH, CDC and FDA (NOT-OD-26-090). A standard Phase II that follows an awarded Phase I is not among the application types the notice lists. Guidance citing NOT-OD-26-073 relies on the April version, which HHS rescinded on July 10. Map every planned application to an institute and a company milestone at the start of the fiscal year, then weigh each resubmission against the new project it would displace.

docs.title: No Late Window
docs.text: A principal investigator's hospital stay in deadline week once gave a company two extra weeks to file. For SBIR and STTR due dates from May 25, 2026, NIH accepts no late application for any personal reason, and relief remains only for a federal system failure that the eRA Service Desk confirms (NOT-OD-26-064). Errors carry the same risk. Grants.gov and eRA Commons check each application on arrival, and a corrected version that lands after 5:00 PM local time counts as late (PA-27-100). Set the internal deadline three business days ahead.

docs.title: Clinical Trials Under One Announcement
docs.text: Teams that once had to pick between a trial-required and a no-trial announcement now file under one, PA-27-100, which accepts both. NIAMS, NIDCR, NCATS, ORIP and every participating FDA center still refuse trials through it, and a trial application that fits only their missions will not be reviewed. Confirm with the program officer at your target institute before designing the trial. Every trial application also needs a Regulatory Plan of up to two pages that names your regulatory contact and the date of each interaction with that authority.

docs.title: Direct to Phase II for STTR
docs.text: A university spinout holding feasibility data from academic grants can now apply for Phase II STTR funding without a Phase I award first (PA-27-102). NIH has offered Direct to Phase II under SBIR for years, regardless of who funded the earlier work, and PA-27-102 extends the same route to STTR. Submit it as a new application. A Phase II that follows an awarded Phase I goes in as a renewal instead.

docs.title: Budget Limits by Institute
docs.text: A Phase I budget built to the SBA guideline of $335,937 sits $364,063 below the $700,000 that NCI allows under PA-27-100. NIA, NIAID, NIGMS, NIMH, NINDS and NCCIH set the same Phase I limit, and eight institutes, including NHLBI, NIDCD and NIDA, accept Phase II budgets up to $3 million. Other institutes hold to the SBA figures, which rose to $335,937 for Phase I and $2,239,578 for Phase II on October 16, 2026 (SBIR.gov). Size the budget to the institute that will likely fund the work. Before requesting more than the SBA guideline, speak with that institute's program staff.

docs.title: Foreign Affiliation Screening
docs.text: One owner's foreign ties can stop an award after the science is scored. During the Just-in-Time stage, NIH collects SBA's foreign affiliation disclosure for every owner and every person who contributes substantively to the project. HHS cannot fund a company that has a parent company, subsidiary or business entity located in China, or an owner or covered individual who is party to a malign foreign talent recruitment program. No chance to resolve a risk is offered once NIH, CDC or FDA identifies it, so review ownership and affiliations before your team starts writing.

docs.title: Writing the Application
docs.text: Six pages is the whole case a Phase I application gets to show why the problem matters, what is new about the answer and how the experiments will prove it (NIH page limits). Phase II and Fast-Track applications get twelve. Every other section either feeds those pages or proves the company can carry the result to market, so write the Specific Aims first and build outward from them.

docs.title: Project Summary and Narrative
docs.text: The Project Summary becomes the public record of the award, since NIH RePORTER publishes the abstract of every funded project. It has 30 lines to state the problem, the product, the aims and the commercial use, written for a scientifically literate reader outside your field. The Project Narrative gets three sentences on relevance to public health. Write it in plain language for a general audience, and name both the patients who benefit and the health outcome you expect to change.

docs.title: Specific Aims
docs.text: One page holds the full argument for the project. Open with the clinical or market gap and the hypothesis that answers it, then list aims that each end in a measurable result. For Phase I, close each aim with the result that would justify a Phase II, stated as a number or a threshold. Avoid aims that depend on each other, because one failed experiment can then sink the whole project.

docs.title: Research Strategy
docs.text: Significance comes first, with the market need set beside the scientific one, because reviewers are asked whether a Phase I project could lead to a marketable product (PA-27-100). Innovation names the products or methods your solution competes with and the advantage it holds over each. Approach carries the preliminary data and the experimental design, along with expected results, benchmarks for success and an alternative for every aim that could fail. A Phase II Approach also has to report what the Phase I work achieved. Phase I applications cannot carry an appendix, so every figure and table that supports feasibility has to fit inside the six pages.

docs.title: Commercialization Plan
docs.text:
A Phase I application may not include one, while every Phase II, Direct to Phase II and Fast-Track application must. NIH allows twelve pages, organized under the section headings its form sets out (NIH Form G.440).

  • Value of the SBIR/STTR Project, Expected Outcomes, and Impact - the need, the Phase III product and how the project fits your business plan, in terms a lay reader can follow.
  • Company - your origins, funding and regulatory history, current products and the management plan for growth.
  • Market, Customer, and Competition - the target customer and the hurdles to adoption, with partners for FDA approval or sales and every competitor you know of.
  • Intellectual Property Protection - how you'll protect what the project produces and hold off competitors once it ends.
  • Finance Plan - how much money commercialization needs, by when, and where it will come from.
  • Production and Marketing Plan - how the product will be made, and the steps you'll take to market and sell it.
  • Revenue Stream - the revenue model, and how staffing changes if the project succeeds.

NIH doesn't require the full twelve pages.

docs.title: Letters of Support
docs.text: NIH encourages you to secure commitments of funds or resources from investors or partners who would help commercialize the product, and those letters belong in the application. Place them in the Letters of Support attachment, after the letters from consultants and collaborators. Ask each writer to state what they will provide and when, since a letter with a figure and a date can be checked against your Finance Plan.

docs.title: Budget Justification
docs.text: Every budget limit under PA-27-100 covers direct costs, indirect costs and fee combined. Reviewers weigh whether the budget and the requested period of support are fully justified for the work proposed, so tie each major cost to a named aim and month.
